practice.sample_answer_en: The speaker argues that an accessible group meeting requires checking timing as well as choosing a suitable room. Two examples illustrate the point: one member needed to leave before a bus departed, while another had a Thursday family responsibility. These are examples of possible constraints, not a schedule that every group should copy. Before booking a room, organizers should ask when members can attend and how long they can stay, then compare those answers with room availability. If one meeting cannot include everyone, the group should separate suitable tasks and explain how decisions will be shared. The main lesson is to build a realistic participation plan rather than assume that an attractive room makes the meeting accessible.
practice.reading_en: Scripted talk for a fictional student workshop: "When we arrange a group meeting, choosing a room is only part of making participation possible. My main point is that timing and access must be checked together. Last month, our project group found a room that everyone liked. However, one member could not stay after four because the last convenient bus left then. Another member had a family duty on Thursdays. These examples do not mean that every group needs the same schedule. They show why a popular room does not guarantee an accessible meeting. Before booking, ask members when they can attend and how long they can stay. Then compare the answers with the room's available times. If no single meeting works, decide which tasks can be completed separately and record how decisions will be shared. A useful plan makes participation realistic rather than merely giving the group an attractive place to meet."

practice.prompt_en: Write a 100-140-word explanation for a new student. Define opportunity cost, explain the rehearsal example, and clarify two boundaries.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以100至140個英文單字向新生解釋機會成本，包含定義、排演例子與兩項適用界線。
practice.sample_answer_en: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when you choose one option. In the workshop example, a student chooses play rehearsal during a free afternoon. If the library workshop would otherwise be the student's preferred activity, its value is the opportunity cost of rehearsing. We do not add the film and every other possible activity, because only one best alternative is being forgone. The concept is also different from a direct payment, such as a rehearsal ticket expense, and it need not involve money. Finally, identifying an opportunity cost does not prove a choice is wrong. Rehearsal may still be the option the student values most.
practice.reading_en: In a fictional planning workshop, a teacher introduces opportunity cost as the value of the best alternative given up when a choice is made. The concept is not limited to money. A student who uses a free afternoon to rehearse a play cannot use the same time for another activity. Suppose the student would otherwise choose a library workshop rather than a film. In that case, the relevant alternative is the workshop, not every possible activity added together. The student may still reasonably choose rehearsal if it matters more to them. Opportunity cost describes a trade-off; it does not automatically identify a mistake or tell everyone which option has greater value. The teacher also distinguishes the rehearsal's ticket expense from the missed workshop opportunity. One is a direct payment, while the other is the value of the best forgone choice. A clear explanation should define the concept, trace the example, and state these boundaries.

questions.prompt_en: What is opportunity cost in the given choice?
questions.answer_en: The value of the library workshop, the best alternative the student gives up.

questions.prompt_en: Why are the film and all other activities not added together?
questions.answer_en: The concept concerns the best forgone alternative, not every possible alternative combined.

questions.prompt_en: Does having an opportunity cost prove rehearsal is a bad decision? Explain.
questions.answer_en: No. The student may value rehearsal more; the concept identifies a trade-off, not an automatic mistake.

practice.prompt_en: Write a 100-140-word description of the fictional trend. Include counts and proportions, explain their contrast, and identify an unanswered causal question.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以100至140個英文單字描述虛構趨勢，列出人數與比例、解釋兩者對比並提出尚未回答的因果問題。
practice.sample_answer_en: The fictional reading-program record shows rising membership counts alongside falling membership proportions. Membership increased from thirty to thirty-six and then forty-two, while total campus enrollment grew from one hundred to one hundred fifty and then two hundred. Consequently, the share of students joining fell from thirty percent to twenty-four percent and then twenty-one percent. There is no contradiction: campus enrollment grew faster than program membership. The figures describe this pattern but do not explain it. For example, they cannot show whether students became less interested or simply lacked information about the program. A useful follow-up would ask members and nonmembers about awareness, scheduling, and barriers before attributing the trend to a particular cause.
practice.reading_en: A fictional campus reading program records membership across three years. In the first year, thirty of one hundred students enrolled in the program. In the second, membership rose to thirty-six while total enrollment at the campus reached one hundred fifty. In the third, forty-two of two hundred students joined. These hypothetical figures show increasing member counts but decreasing membership proportions: thirty percent, twenty-four percent, and twenty-one percent. A headline saying "Participation fell every year" would be ambiguous because the number of members actually rose. A clearer description separates the two measures. The record does not explain the pattern. Changes in student interests, recruitment, scheduling, or other factors might matter, but none was measured. The program should therefore avoid attributing the trend to one cause. If it wants to investigate participation, it could gather information about awareness and barriers among members and nonmembers. That inquiry would address reasons that the membership totals alone cannot establish.

practice.prompt_en: Write a 100-140-word discussion contribution. Acknowledge the current evidence, identify an assumption, ask a focused question, and explain why its answer matters.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以100至140個英文單字寫討論發言，承認現有證據、指出假設、提出聚焦問題並解釋答案為何重要。
practice.sample_answer_en: The laptop test gives us useful evidence that the guide's pages can be navigated easily under those conditions. However, the proposed use is different: incoming students would consult the guide on phones while moving around campus. Are we assuming that success on a laptop transfers directly to smaller screens and limited mobile data? My focused question is whether the team has tested the guide on phones under those intended conditions. If it has, the results could help us judge the proposal more accurately. If it has not, a short practical test would address the gap. I am not claiming the guide will fail; I want the evidence to match the situation in which students will actually use it.
practice.reading_en: A fictional orientation team proposes replacing printed campus guides with a mobile guide. Six volunteers tested the guide on their own laptops and found the pages easy to navigate. The team concludes that all incoming students will be able to use it conveniently while walking around campus. During discussion, Amy notices an assumption: success on a laptop is being treated as evidence of success on phones in outdoor conditions. She first acknowledges the useful navigation feedback, then asks whether the guide has been tested on smaller screens with limited mobile data. This question does not claim that the guide will fail. It identifies a specific gap that matters to the proposed use. A vague challenge such as "Is this really a good idea?" would give the team less direction. A productive answer could describe existing phone tests or propose a small test under the intended conditions. The discussion can then address evidence rather than defend a general impression.

objectives_zh_TW: 先準確回應他人論點，再延伸或質疑。

practice.prompt_en: Write a 100-140-word seminar contribution. Build on Sam's point, challenge the exclusive-format conclusion with evidence, and suggest a shared next step.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以100至140個英文單字寫研討發言，承接Sam的論點，以證據質疑僅用數位的結論，並建議共同下一步。
practice.sample_answer_en: Sam's example shows a useful benefit of digital files: searching can help students locate key terms quickly. I agree that we should preserve that feature. However, I question whether it supports using digital materials exclusively. In our fictional access check, four of eighteen classmates shared a device at home, and two reported unreliable internet; those groups may overlap. This suggests that convenience during a classroom activity does not guarantee access outside class. Could we keep downloadable files and offer a printed option while checking which students need it? We should also avoid adding the two counts without knowing the overlap. This approach retains the documented search benefit while responding to a separate access concern.
practice.reading_en: In a fictional seminar, students discuss whether a course should use only digital reading materials. Sam argues that searchable files make it easier to locate key terms. He refers to a practice activity in which students quickly found definitions using the search function. Amy agrees that search can help, but challenges the move from that benefit to an exclusively digital format. In a separate fictional access check, four of eighteen classmates reported sharing a device at home, and two described unreliable internet connections. The groups may overlap, so the numbers cannot simply be added to count all affected students. Amy proposes keeping downloadable files while offering a printed option. Sam replies that the search activity did not measure access outside class and agrees that this issue needs attention. The discussion progresses because Amy acknowledges the original point, introduces relevant evidence, and questions the scope of the conclusion rather than dismissing Sam or denying the search benefit.

practice.prompt_en: Write a 100-140-word presentation script recommending a limited equipment-desk trial. Use spoken signposts, concise evidence, a qualification, and a clear conclusion; rehearse it aloud.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以100至140個英文單字寫器材櫃台試行短講，包含口頭路標、精簡證據、限定及清楚結論，並朗讀演練。
practice.sample_answer_en: I recommend a short Wednesday trial of a later equipment-desk hour. First, the current schedule may not match some practical classes: twelve of thirty students in a hypothetical survey said late lessons had caused them to miss the desk. This reports a problem, not guaranteed demand for the new hour. Second, the manager could support the trial by opening later that morning, so morning users must also be considered. We should record visits during both periods and ask affected students about access. To conclude, the trial would let us compare benefits and costs before changing the regular schedule. It is a way to test a possible improvement, not a promise that every student will benefit.
practice.reading_en: Scripted presentation for a fictional campus forum: "I recommend testing a later opening time for the equipment desk on one weekday. First, our current schedule ends before some practical classes finish. In a hypothetical survey of thirty students from those classes, twelve said they had missed the desk because their lessons ended late. This does not prove that all twelve would use a later service, but it identifies a possible scheduling mismatch. Second, the desk manager says a later hour could be tried on Wednesday if the opening hour that morning moved back. We therefore need to consider students who use the morning service as well. My proposal is a short Wednesday trial, with records of both morning and late visits. To conclude, a limited trial would let us examine the trade-off before making a permanent change. The purpose is to test a possible solution, not to promise that one schedule will suit everyone."

questions.prompt_en: What specific change does the speaker recommend testing?
questions.answer_en: A later equipment-desk hour on Wednesday, with a corresponding later morning opening.

questions.prompt_en: How do First, Second, and To conclude help listeners?
questions.answer_en: They signal the problem evidence, feasibility and trade-off, and final recommendation.

questions.prompt_en: Why should the trial record morning visits as well as late visits?
questions.answer_en: The later morning opening may affect existing morning users, so both sides of the trade-off matter.

practice.prompt_en: Write a 100-140-word spoken answer to the examination-results question. Answer directly, cite the actual evidence, state uncertainty, and suggest a responsible next step.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以100至140個英文單字寫對考試成效追問的口頭回答，直接作答、引用實際證據、說明未知並建議負責任的下一步。
practice.sample_answer_en: We do not yet know whether the workshop improved examination results. Our evidence is narrower: sixteen of twenty participants reported feeling more organized afterward. That feedback describes their experience, but it does not measure scores or establish a comparison with students who did not attend. I would therefore avoid promising an examination benefit. The positive responses do give us a reason to consider further testing of the workshop. Before doing that, we should define which outcome we want to examine and decide how to collect appropriate evidence with permission. If examination performance is the question, the study design must address that outcome directly rather than treating a different positive response as proof.
practice.reading_en: After a fictional presentation about a study-skills workshop, a listener asks whether the workshop improved examination results. The presenter has feedback forms from twenty participants, sixteen of whom said they felt more organized afterward. However, the team did not collect examination scores or compare participants with students who did not attend. A direct answer is therefore, "We do not yet know whether examination results improved." The presenter can then explain that the available evidence concerns self-reported organization, which is a different outcome. Another listener asks why a second workshop is worth considering. The presenter can point to the positive feedback as a reason for further testing, while avoiding a promise of higher scores. A useful follow-up plan would define the desired outcome and collect appropriate evidence with permission. The exchange demonstrates that a clear answer can include uncertainty. Repeating the presentation or changing the topic would leave the listener's actual question unresolved.

practice.sample_answer_en:
Subject: Request for feedback on our project conclusion
Dear Dr. Chen,
Our group is preparing a presentation about library access using a facilities note and a small class survey. Could we meet for ten minutes during your Tuesday consultation hour to check whether our conclusion stays within the evidence? We can send a one-page outline beforehand, with the survey questions and proposed recommendation. Our draft is due Friday, so feedback by Wednesday would help us revise it. If a meeting is unavailable, a brief written comment on the outline would also be useful. We will wait for confirmation before considering the appointment booked.
Thank you for considering our request.
Sincerely,
The student project group

Subject: Question about presenting our library-access project
Dear Dr. Chen,
Our student group is preparing a short presentation for the campus learning forum. We have compared a facilities note with a small class survey and would like advice on explaining the limits of our evidence. Could we book ten minutes during your consultation hour next Tuesday to ask whether our conclusion matches the sources? We can send a one-page outline in advance, including the survey questions and the exact claims we plan to make. The forum draft is due on Friday, so a response by Wednesday would help us revise it in time. If Tuesday is unavailable, we would appreciate another appointment or a brief written comment on the outline. We understand that the requested time may not be possible and will wait for confirmation before treating any meeting as booked.
Thank you for considering our request.
Sincerely,

objectives_zh_TW: 以具體困難、行動與證據組織反思。
區分個人經驗的改善與普遍有效主張。

episodes.parent_tip_zh_TW: 反思不是只說「我學到了很多」；要讓讀者看見你改了什麼，以及哪些跡象支持進步。

practice.prompt_en: Write a 100-140-word first-person reflection as Amy. Describe the difficulty, revisions, evidence of partial progress, and a next step without overgeneralizing.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以Amy第一人稱寫100至140個英文單字的反思，交代困難、修訂、部分進步證據與下一步，避免過度推論。
practice.sample_answer_en: My first research presentation made its recommendation difficult to identify. Two classmates' feedback led me to write a one-sentence claim, give each slide one purpose, and move detailed evidence into my notes. In the next rehearsal, both classmates could state my recommendation, which suggests that this draft became clearer for them. However, one still confused a survey finding with my proposed solution. I added phrases that identify the source before reporting evidence and mark my own recommendation separately. I cannot conclude that shorter slides always work better from this small experience. My next step is to rehearse with someone unfamiliar with the topic and ask them to distinguish the findings from my analysis.
practice.reading_en: In a fictional learning journal, Amy describes revising her first research presentation. Her initial slides contained long paragraphs, and two classmates said they could not identify the main recommendation. Amy responded by writing a one-sentence claim, reducing each slide to one purpose, and moving detailed evidence into speaker notes. During a second rehearsal, both classmates could state the recommendation accurately, but one still confused a survey result with Amy's own proposed solution. Amy therefore added spoken phrases such as "the survey reports" and "I recommend" to distinguish evidence from analysis. She does not claim that shorter slides always produce better presentations or that two classmates represent every audience. Instead, she treats their responses as useful feedback on this particular draft. Her next step is to rehearse with a listener unfamiliar with the topic and ask that listener to separate the source findings from her recommendation. The reflection connects a problem, an action, evidence of partial progress, and a remaining learning need.

questions.prompt_en: What change helped clarify Amy's recommendation?
questions.answer_en: She wrote a one-sentence claim, gave each slide one purpose, and moved details to notes.

questions.prompt_en: What remaining problem did the second rehearsal reveal?
questions.answer_en: One classmate confused a survey finding with Amy's proposed solution.

questions.prompt_en: Why is an unfamiliar listener a relevant next step?
questions.answer_en: That listener can test clarity without prior knowledge, especially the distinction between findings and recommendations.

practice.prompt_en: Write a 100-140-word source-based paragraph. Attribute a careful paraphrase of Lane, quote Mo briefly and exactly, and distinguish your own synthesis from both sources.
practice.prompt_zh_TW: 以100至140個英文單字寫來源式段落，標示Lane的審慎改寫，準確短引Mo，並區分自己的整合與來源內容。
practice.sample_answer_en: In the fictional note "Finding Books," librarian Lane suggests that clearer shelf labels may help new readers locate broad subject areas. This claim concerns one orientation session and does not establish faster searching for every reader. Instructor Mo offers a different emphasis in "Beyond the Shelf": "Clear labels cannot replace an accurate catalog." Mo distinguishes general locations from information about specific items and their availability. My analysis is that the two tools serve complementary purposes: labels can guide a reader toward a subject area, while an accurate catalog supports a more specific search. This synthesis draws on both notes, but it should not be presented as a joint recommendation explicitly made by Lane and Mo.
practice.reading_en:
Two fictional source notes are provided for a writing exercise. In "Finding Books," librarian Lane reports that clearer shelf labels may help new readers locate broad subject areas. The note describes one orientation session and does not measure total search time. In "Beyond the Shelf," instructor Mo writes, "Clear labels cannot replace an accurate catalog." Mo explains that labels show general locations, while a catalog identifies specific items and whether they are available.
A responsible writer can paraphrase Lane's point as a possible benefit for locating subject areas, but should not claim that Lane proved faster searching for every reader. The short quotation from Mo must retain its exact wording and be attributed. The writer may then offer an original analysis: labels and an accurate catalog appear to serve complementary purposes. That analysis combines the notes; it is not a sentence both authors explicitly wrote. Clear attribution lets readers distinguish reported ideas, quoted language, and the student's own reasoning.

practice.sample_answer_en: Our inquiry asks how clarification questions differ between two instruction versions for a short classroom task. One version will include a numbered checklist, while both describe the same requirements. Two groups will use different versions and exchange them for a similar task later. Observers will use consistent categories to record questions, and we will compare those records with completed work and participant comments. These additional sources matter because silence does not necessarily show understanding. The design remains limited: groups may differ in experience, and practice from the first task may influence the second. We will therefore describe the patterns in this class and consider alternative explanations rather than claim that checklists always cause clearer understanding.
practice.reading_en: A fictional writing class wants to investigate whether assignment instructions are clear. Instead of asking the broad question "What makes all instructions effective?", students plan a small comparison of two instruction versions for a ten-minute practice task. Both versions describe the same task, but one includes a numbered checklist. Two small groups will use different versions during the first session and exchange versions for a similar task later. Observers will record the number and type of clarification questions, using the same categories each time. They will also ask participants which wording caused confusion. The plan is feasible within class time, but it has limits. The groups may differ in experience, and doing a similar task twice may itself reduce questions. Fewer questions could also reflect reluctance to ask rather than better understanding. The students therefore plan to compare question records with completed work and participant comments. Their findings will describe this small inquiry, not establish a universal rule for every learning context.

practice.prompt_en: Write a proposal and a three-sentence spoken version, 100-140 words total. Use both sources, recommend a limited trial, preserve one uncertainty, and rehearse the spoken version.

practice.sample_answer_en:
Proposal: I recommend a limited orientation-guide trial using the support office's smaller text guide and optional printed maps. Source A reports slow downloads for three of twelve students, while Source B offers twenty printed copies but gives no evidence of demand. We should compare access to the smaller guide with the current map and record requests for paper copies. Eventual arrival does not prove equal convenience, so the trial should also ask about delays.
Spoken version: I recommend testing the smaller guide while keeping printed maps available. The sources identify a download problem and possible support, but neither proves what every student needs. Recording access difficulties and print requests will help us decide the next step.
practice.reading_en:
Source A is a fictional orientation-guide trial with twelve incoming students. Nine reported that the phone map opened quickly, while three reported slow downloads. All twelve eventually found the meeting point, but the team did not measure completion time or test every phone model. The note recommends investigating the slow downloads before wider use.
Source B is a fictional support-office note. Staff can print twenty simple maps for the next orientation event and update a text-based guide with a smaller file size than the current map before it begins. However, they cannot provide a person at the entrance throughout the whole event. The note describes resources, not student preferences.
A final communication project should combine the user experience with the available support rather than assume that either source supplies the complete solution. A short trial could compare the smaller guide with the current map and record requests for printed copies. A written proposal and spoken version should preserve the same evidence limits: eventual arrival does not prove equal convenience, and printing capacity does not establish demand.

questions.answer_en: Twenty simple printed maps and an updated small text-based guide, but no continuous entrance staffing.

questions.prompt_en: What should a trial measure to connect both sources?
